output.summary: The diff replaces requiredRoles.every(role => userRoles.includes(role)) with requiredRoles.some(role => userRoles.includes(role)) in src/access.ts. This inverts the documented authorization semantics and does not preserve behavior. It violates the contract in two ways: (1) access now requires only one of the required roles rather than all of them, and (2) an empty requiredRoles array now denies access instead of permitting it. Both defects are introduced by the single changed line and are high-confidence.

findings.title: Authorization weakened: every replaced by some grants access with any single required role
findings.body: The contract states 'Access requires every role in requiredRoles, not just one.' The original implementation used Array.prototype.every, which requires the user to hold all required roles. The changed implementation uses Array.prototype.some, which returns true as soon as the user holds any one of the required roles, granting access to users who are missing other required roles. This is an authorization bypass / access-control regression introduced by the diff.
findings.evidence: src/access.ts line 2 now reads: return requiredRoles.some(role => userRoles.includes(role)); The diff replaced requiredRoles.every(role => userRoles.includes(role)) with requiredRoles.some(...).
findings.suggestion: Revert the change to return requiredRoles.every(role => userRoles.includes(role));

findings.title: Empty requiredRoles now denies access instead of permitting it
findings.body: The contract states 'If requiredRoles is empty, access is permitted.' Array.prototype.every on an empty array returns true (vacuously satisfying all requirements), but Array.prototype.some on an empty array returns false. The changed implementation therefore denies access when requiredRoles is empty, breaking the documented empty-requirements behavior.
findings.evidence: src/access.ts line 2 now reads: return requiredRoles.some(role => userRoles.includes(role)); Array.prototype.some returns false for an empty array, whereas the contract requires access to be permitted when requiredRoles is empty.
findings.suggestion: Revert the change to return requiredRoles.every(role => userRoles.includes(role));, which returns true for an empty requiredRoles array.

output.diagnosis: The diff changed the authorization predicate from every to some, inverting both required behaviors: access now requires only one of the required roles instead of all, and an empty requiredRoles list now yields false (denied) instead of true (permitted).
